Forgotten figures

Christine Ladd-Franklin, the doctor without a degree

She finished her thesis in 1882 but was not awarded her doctorate until 1926 because she was a woman.

Christine Ladd-Franklin studied mathematics and logic at Johns Hopkins University, which she was allowed to attend as an exception. In 1882 she met all the requirements for a doctorate, but the university did not award degrees to women. She received it in 1926, at the age of 78.

A theory of colour

Besides logic, she was interested in vision. She studied in Germany with Georg Elias Müller and in Berlin with Arthur König, though only as an auditor. In 1892 she proposed an evolutionary theory of colour vision: first we would have seen in black and white, then distinguished blue and yellow, and finally red and green.

She also clashed with Edward Titchener, who would not admit women to his group of experimental psychologists. She wrote to him for years in protest, without success. Her case reflects the barriers women faced in the early days of psychology.

References

  1. Furumoto, L. (1992). Joining separate spheres: Christine Ladd-Franklin, woman-scientist (1847–1930). American Psychologist, 47(2), 175–182.
